**Setup:**
- VIF-A advertises: `10.10.1.0/24` → covers `10.10.1.0 – 10.10.1.255`
- VIF-B advertises: `10.10.0.0/22` → covers `10.10.0.0 – 10.10.3.255`

The /22 fully contains four /24s:
- `10.10.0.0/24`
- `10.10.1.0/24` ← also covered by VIF-A
- `10.10.2.0/24`
- `10.10.3.0/24`

**If VIF-B fails:**

- `10.10.1.0/24` — **stays reachable**, since VIF-A independently advertises this exact block. This is your only overlap/failover coverage.
- `10.10.0.0/24`, `10.10.2.0/24`, `10.10.3.0/24` — **at risk / unreachable via DX**, since nothing else advertises these ranges. Traffic to these three /24s (75% of the /22's address space) would have no DX path and would fall back to any other route (internet/VPN) if one exists, or blackhole if not.

**Bottom line:** VIF-A only backs up a quarter of what VIF-B carries. There's no true failover for `10.10.0.0/24`, `10.10.2.0/24`, or `10.10.3.0/24` — if you need full redundancy for the /22, VIF-A (or another VIF) needs to advertise the whole `10.10.0.0/22`, not just the `.1.0/24` slice.
